INTRO_TITLE: Use Case: Lobby Art & Development Launches
INTRO_COL1: Oddtoe is an experiential design and generative-AI animation studio based in Melbourne, creating projection, installation, and animated work for events, venues, and galleries. This is a use case: how a developer, an architect or an interior designer uses Oddtoe for lobby art and a development launch, from the first drawing to the day the piece is handed over. The worked example is a commissioned piece for the lobby of a new building. The same steps apply to a mural on the hoarding, a garden on the podium, a projection for launch night, or a piece that satisfies a public-art condition.
INTRO_COL2: You are asking on behalf of a client, so the picture has to exist before the piece does. That suits the way Oddtoe works. The piece gets drawn in the architect’s section, at scale, with people standing next to it, and your client approves that drawing before anything is cut. The builder gets working drawings with the fixings and the power marked on them. On launch night the same design goes up as projection on the site for the press and the first buyers. After handover the piece stays for the life of the building, with maintenance notes for whoever looks after it.
DRAWINGS_KICKER: Let's look at three steps in the process...
DRAWINGS_INTRO: Oddtoe can handle the first three stages of a lobby piece: where the idea comes from, how it gets drawn at scale in the building so your client can approve it, and how it fixes to the structure and what services it needs, worked out with your builder.
DRAW1_BODY: What is the one thing people photograph in this lobby? What does the building get called because of it? I start with the site plan and the section, the client’s brief, and whatever the interior scheme already promises. The idea has to suit the building and read from the street through the glass. A form like this one starts as a quick schematic before anyone commits to it.
DRAW2_BODY: The piece drawn at scale, with figures beside it, front and side, in the same section the architect uses. The client signs off on this drawing. Nothing gets built until it is agreed on paper, and if the ceiling height or the column grid changes, the drawing changes first.
DRAW3_BODY: Working out how the piece attaches to the building: floor fixings, a ceiling hang, a plinth, a power point for the lighting, and whether it comes through the doors in one piece or in sections. Here a form is carved in the studio before its finish goes on. Oddtoe works this out with your builder while the fit-out is still on the drawings.

PANEL_TITLE: What a Lobby Piece Does for the Building
PANEL_INTRO: A projection on the display suite on launch night, then a piece in the lobby that turns up in every listing photograph for as long as the building stands. What does that do for your client’s numbers? Quite a lot, and it can be counted: the press that ran the picture, enquiries in the weeks after the launch, and the photographs the agents use for every sale and lease after that.
PANEL_ITEM1_TEXT: Outlets that ran the launch-night picture, and how many people they reach
PANEL_ITEM2_TEXT: Display-suite appointments and enquiries in the weeks after, against the weeks before
PANEL_ITEM3_TEXT: The piece in the agent's photographs, the website and the brochure, for every sale and lease that follows
PANEL_OUTRO: I like the tracking in place before the night. Oddtoe shares a founder with the Datalabs Agency, a data visualisation studio, so a dashboard that shows what the launch did for enquiries can be part of the job.
CIRCLES_TITLE: 6 JOBS ONE BUILDING GIVES AN ARTIST
CIRCLES_SUB: Six things a developer or an architect would commission over the life of one project. Roll over a circle and pick the one your client needs.
CIRCLES_FOOT: Want one of these for a building? Send the plans and the date. The same design can go on the hoarding, up as the launch projection, and into the lobby.
CIRCLE1_BODY: One sculpture, kinetic work or topiary form in the lobby that gives the building its photograph and, if it is good enough, its name. Drawn in the architect’s section first, so your client approves a picture before anything gets made.
CIRCLE2_BODY: Eighteen months of construction fence with nothing on it. A mural or a drawn story along the hoarding gives the street something to look at every day, and the same characters turn up inside when the building opens.
CIRCLE3_BODY: Projection on the site or on the display suite for one evening, for the press and the first buyers. The building appears at full size before it exists, and everyone photographs it with the street behind.
CIRCLE4_BODY: The council wants a percentage spent on public art and the architect wants something worth standing next to. A commissioned piece can do both, and the drawings go to the planner before the money is spent.
CIRCLE5_BODY: A sensory garden or topiary on the podium or in the courtyard, planted to a drawing and shaped over the years. A character grown in hedge is the slowest sculpture there is, and the residents get to watch it grow.
CIRCLE6_BODY: An animated walk through the building for the sales suite, drawn like a picture book instead of rendered like a catalogue. It looks like a place people will live in, and buyers remember it.
WHO_COL1: Developers, architects, interior designers, landscape architects, and the sales teams behind a development. What they all have is a building with a date and a client who has to approve a picture first. Developers have a launch for each project and a display suite that has to sell off the plan for a year. They want one thing the press photographs on the night and the agents use for years after. Architects have a lobby, an atrium or a forecourt to finish, and sometimes a council condition to spend a percentage of the budget on public art.
WHO_COL2: Interior designers want a piece that belongs to the scheme, at a size the catalogues do not sell, drawn in their own section so it can go to the client with the rest of the presentation. Landscape architects come for the podium and the courtyard: a sensory garden, topiary, or a sculpture that stands up to the weather and to children climbing on it. Building managers and owners’ corporations arrive later, when a finished building has an empty lobby and a budget. Oddtoe works for all of them, and for the agencies presenting on their behalf.
TIMELINE_TITLE: A LOBBY PIECE, FROM BRIEF TO HANDOVER
STEP1_TITLE: The lobby is finished, and it is empty
STEP1_BODY: The fit-out is done, the stone is down, the lights are on, and the space everyone walks through looks like a hotel nobody has checked into. The launch is in the diary and the agents need a photograph that is not a render. So before anything gets drawn we settle one question with your client: what is the one thing this building is known for?
STEP1_CRAFT: Reading the plans, and the client, before drawing anything
STEP1_CAPTION: The brief, before anything is drawn
STEP2_TITLE: Drawn in your section, at scale
STEP2_BODY: I draw the piece into the architect’s own section and plan, at scale, with figures standing beside it, so it can sit in the presentation with everything else. Your client approves that drawing. If the ceiling drops or the column grid moves, the drawing moves first and nothing has been cut. That picture is what you present to a third party before the piece exists.
STEP2_CRAFT: Scale drawings in the architect’s own section
STEP2_CAPTION: Drawn flat, with figures for scale
STEP3_TITLE: Built to the drawings, fixed with the builder
STEP3_BODY: Design happens in Melbourne. The build happens in my workshop for a carved or built piece, or with a specialist maker for topiary, metalwork or an inflatable, working from the same drawings. Fixings, a plinth, power for the lighting and the route through the doors get worked out with your builder while the fit-out is still on paper, so nothing is drilled twice.
STEP3_CAPTION: A form carved in the studio, before the finish goes on
STEP4_TITLE: The building at full size, before it exists
STEP4_BODY: Projection on the site or on the display suite for one evening, for the press and the first buyers. Whatever is going into the lobby goes up on the wall at building scale, and the picture the agents want gets taken that night, with the street behind it.
STEP4_CAPTION: A sculpture lit by projection for one evening
STEP5_BODY: The piece goes in, gets fixed and lit, and is photographed properly. The handover pack has the as-built drawings, the maintenance notes, and the name of whoever built each part, so the building manager in ten years knows what it is and how to clean it. That is the last day I am needed on site.
STEP5_CAPTION: A walk-in form installed indoors, on a timber floor
STEP6_BODY: Every sale and every lease gets photographed with the piece in it, for as long as the building stands. Residents give directions by it. If it is good enough, the building gets called after it, and that lasts a lot longer than anything that happened on launch night.
STEP6_CRAFT: Made once, for the life of the building
STEP6_CAPTION: A Melbourne building known by its facade, decades on
WHY_KICKER: The bit that is not a service
WHY_COL1: Most of what I make is up for a night or a week and then goes back in the crate. A lobby piece is the other kind. It stays, and the same people walk past it every morning for twenty years. That is closer to public sculpture than to an event, and public sculpture is what I want to be making anyway. I came to sculpture through street art, which is punk rock for visual artists: no gallery, no permission, and seen by people who never decided to look at art that day.
WHY_COL2: A lobby is the sanctioned version of the same thing. Nobody goes there for art. They go to collect a parcel or wait for a lift, and the piece has to earn its place with someone who is in a hurry. I find that a much more interesting test than a gallery wall. The practical upside for your client is that the person drawing the piece has a stake in whether it lasts. I want it to still look right in ten years for the same reason you do, and I would like my name on it.

WYG_TITLE: What Does Your Client Actually Get?
WYG_COL1: The piece, installed and lit, the drawings it was approved and built from, the launch-night projection, and the photographs and maintenance notes to hand to the building manager. • The piece — in this example a lobby sculpture, fixed, lit and photographed • The drawings — the approval drawing in the architect’s section, and the working drawings the builder used • Launch night — projection on the site or the display suite, with the footage afterwards • Handover — as-built drawings, maintenance notes, and who built each part
WYG_COL2: People tend to forget the drawings. Because the piece is designed before it is built, your client also owns artwork that works on the hoarding, in the brochure and in the sales suite without redrawing anything. It can be whatever the building needs: a sculpture, a kinetic piece that moves with the air from the doors, topiary or a sensory garden on the podium, a mural along the hoarding, or the same design animated as a drawn fly-through for the sales suite. They are designed together, so what is on the fence is the same piece that ends up in the lobby.
PKG1_KICKER: What is the building known for?
PKG1_BODY: We work out what the lobby needs to say before we work out what to build. Bring the plans, the launch date, and whatever the interior scheme already promises.
PKG2_KICKER: Drawn until your client can see it
PKG2_BODY: The piece drawn in the architect’s section, at scale, with figures beside it. Your client signs off on a picture of the thing in the finished lobby, before it exists.
PKG3_KICKER: Fixed, lit, and through the doors?
PKG3_BODY: Weight and fixings. Power for the lighting. Whether it fits through the doors or arrives in sections. The council’s public-art condition, if there is one. And the launch date.
PKG4_BODY: Designed in Melbourne, built by the right maker for the piece, here or near the site. Finished for a lobby, where people touch it, and fixed the way the builder and I agreed on paper.
PKG5_BODY: I run the job myself: visual progress reports your client can forward, a schedule against the launch date, and the handover pack with the drawings and the maintenance notes.
CRED_TITLE: Who Designs This, and What Has Been Built
CRED_COL1: Oddtoe designs and builds sculpture. The lines a building brief draws on are kinetic sculpture, topiary, sensory gardens, and murals. Two built precedents, both in Melbourne. A wall mural in Brunswick, on a street people walk down every day, and still there. And a 2.1-metre baobab, carved, finished and lit by live projection, designed and built for Babbling with Baobabs, a kids’ comedy show at the Melbourne Comedy Festival in 2019, at Signal, a City of Melbourne venue.
CRED_COL2: The baobab was drawn first, approved on paper, built in the studio, and installed in a venue with its own rules about fixings and power. The same hand draws all of it, which is how the hoarding, the lobby piece and the garden can belong to one building. Your lobby piece goes through the same sequence, with a builder in the room instead of a stage manager. Where this page describes something I have not built yet, it describes the process: Oddtoe designs, and a specialist maker builds from the drawings.

FAQ.q: What does this lobby art and development launch use case cover?
FAQ.a: A worked example of a lobby commission. It follows one brief - a new building with a finished, empty lobby and a launch date - from the first drawing through client approval, fabrication, launch night, and handover with maintenance notes. The example is a commissioned piece for the lobby. A mural on the hoarding, a garden on the podium or a projection for the launch would follow the same steps.

FAQ.q: How long does a lobby art commission take?
FAQ.a: [Oddtoe: fill] from brief to installation for a built piece. Design and your client’s approval come first, then fabrication, then the install, which is scheduled with the builder around the fit-out. Topiary and a garden run on their own clock, because plants do. The launch-night projection can be ready before the piece is, since it is made from the same drawings.

Oddtoe does not publish prices. Cost is driven by what the piece is, how large, what it is made from, how it fixes to the building, and whether a specialist maker is involved. It is costed the same way as any other prop fabrication job. Send the plans and the date and you get a quote your client can read.

FAQ.q: Can the piece be built interstate or overseas?
FAQ.a: Yes. The design is done in Melbourne and the build can happen in my workshop, with a specialist maker, or with a fabricator near the site working from the drawings. If it ships, it is designed to crate, and freight, customs and any treatment the materials need are worked through with a freight agent as part of the job.

FAQ.q: Does the piece stay, or can it be moved?
FAQ.a: It is designed to stay: fixed, lit, handed over with maintenance notes, and meant to be there for the life of the building. If your client wants something that moves between buildings, or a launch piece that comes down after the campaign, say so at the brief and it gets designed to come apart instead.

FAQ.q: Can Oddtoe do the development launch projection and animation as well?
FAQ.a: Yes, and they are designed together. One set of drawings becomes the lobby piece, the projection on the site or the display suite on launch night, and the drawn fly-through for the sales suite, which is made with generative AI animation.

FAQ.q: Can a commissioned piece satisfy a council public-art condition?
FAQ.a: Often, yes, and it is worth raising at the brief. Councils differ on what counts, who has to be consulted, and what has to be visible from the street. What I can do is draw the piece for the planner at the same time as for your client, so the condition is settled on paper before anything is built. Whether it satisfies a particular council is that council’s call.
Oddtoe is based in Melbourne, Australia. Supplier and business contacts run through Berlin and Los Angeles, and those are the starting points for work in Europe and the United States.
